key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn to call tools for the wrong reason, using superficial prompt cues instead of true task need.
engineering_relevance: For reliable agent systems, tool-use policies should be trained and audited for causal necessity, not just task success, to avoid brittle shortcut behavior.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with injected cue–tool correlations during training.
Evaluated counterfactual cases where cues remained but the tool was unnecessary to expose shortcut tool use.
Added a dense tool-necessity reward using an LLM judge to score whether each call was actually warranted.
evidence_signal: In counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation increased by up to 39%, and shortcut learning appeared only after the agent had already learned the tool reliably.
watch_item: Using an LLM judge for tool-necessity rewards may introduce judge bias or calibration errors, so it needs careful validation.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
